description: Christian pilgrimage sites, Christmas and Easter, mission, and the worldwide Church.
content_html:
Christian Pilgrimage

Pilgrimage is a journey made to a sacred place for spiritual reasons. Christians have practised pilgrimage since the earliest centuries. The spec names four sites:

  • Jerusalem: The holiest site in Christianity, where Jesus was crucified, buried and raised. Pilgrims visit the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, the Via Dolorosa and the Garden of Gethsemane. Jerusalem is also holy to Jews and Muslims, making it a place of both spiritual depth and ongoing geo-political complexity.
  • Iona (Scotland): A small island off the west coast of Scotland where St Columba founded a monastery in 563 CE. The Iona Community (founded 1938 by George MacLeod) has made it a centre of ecumenical spirituality and social justice Christianity. Pilgrims come for retreat, reflection and the experience of Celtic spirituality.
  • Taizé (France): An ecumenical community founded in 1940 by Brother Roger Schutz. Each year tens of thousands of young people from across the world visit Taizé for prayer, song and reconciliation. Its simple, repetitive chants have become widely used across denominations. Taizé emphasises unity between Catholics and Protestants.
  • Walsingham (England): England’s national Marian shrine, dating to 1061. After destruction at the Reformation, it was restored in the twentieth century and is now visited by both Catholics and Anglicans. It represents the healing of divisions between denominations.

Luke 2:41–43 provides a biblical basis for pilgrimage: the young Jesus goes with his parents to Jerusalem for the Passover, showing that visiting sacred sites is part of faithful Jewish (and, by extension, Christian) practice.

Catholics and Orthodox strongly affirm pilgrimage as spiritually meritorious. Protestant reformers (Luther, Calvin) were more cautious: they rejected the idea that visiting a physical location earns spiritual credit, arguing God is present everywhere. Modern Protestants vary: some travel to Israel for educational reasons without claiming spiritual merit; others, like those visiting Iona or Taizé, do so for community and renewal rather than indulgences.

Christian Festivals: Christmas and Easter

Christmas celebrates the Incarnation — God becoming human in Jesus. The liturgical season of Advent begins four Sundays before Christmas and is a time of spiritual preparation and expectation. Christmas Day (25 December in Western churches) celebrates the birth of Jesus. The Christmas story combines Matthew 2 (Magi, Herod, Egypt) and Luke 2 (shepherds, manger, Bethlehem).

Easter is the most important Christian festival, celebrating Christ’s resurrection. It is preceded by Holy Week: Palm Sunday (entry into Jerusalem), Maundy Thursday (Last Supper, washing of feet), Good Friday (crucifixion), Holy Saturday (the waiting), Easter Sunday (resurrection).

1 Corinthians 15:12–34 is Paul’s great defence of the resurrection: “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins.” Paul argues the entire Christian hope rests on the historical reality of the resurrection. Without it, Christianity collapses.

Key Fact

1 Corinthians 15:12–34: Paul argues that if Christ has not been raised, faith is “futile.” The resurrection of Jesus is the guarantee of Christians’ own future resurrection. Easter celebrates this as historical fact, not symbol.

Mission, Evangelism and the Future of the Church

Mission is the Church’s outward movement into the world. Evangelism is the direct proclamation of the Gospel. Mark 16:9–20 (the so-called ‘longer ending’) records the risen Jesus commissioning his disciples: “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.” The spec includes this as the basis for Christian missionary work.

The Local and Worldwide Church

The local church serves its immediate community. This includes: regular Sunday worship as the centre of Christian identity; outreach work (food banks, community cafes, debt counselling); ecumenism (working across denominations in shared projects); and pastoral care for individuals.

The worldwide Church works for reconciliation and supports persecuted Christians. Christian Aid is the named development agency in this spec. It works in partnership with local organisations across the Global South on relief and development, grounded in Matthew 25:31–46 (the Sheep and Goats): Christians are called to see Christ in “the least of these.”

Key Fact

Christian Aid operates in over 40 countries, tackling poverty through long-term development. Its work is grounded in Matthew 25:31–46. The local church’s community role includes food banks, outreach work and ecumenical partnerships.

These two sites are Edexcel-specific pilgrimage sites not commonly found in other GCSE specifications. Iona is significant as the birthplace of Scottish Christianity and a centre of Celtic spirituality and social justice. Taizé is significant as an ecumenical community drawing hundreds of thousands of young Christians annually, representing hope for unity between Catholic and Protestant churches. Both are alternatives to the traditional ‘relic-and-indulgence’ model of pilgrimage — their significance is more about community and spiritual renewal than seeking miraculous healing.
exam_tip_html: Iona and Taizé are Edexcel-specific sites — know what makes each distinctive (Iona: Celtic spirituality, social justice, founded by Columba 563 CE; Taizé: ecumenical, Brother Roger 1940, young people, unity). For the 12-mark Discuss on mission: “The most important work of the Christian Church is mission and evangelism.” Develop for (the Great Commission; 1 Corinthians 15 ties everything to resurrection and proclamation) and against (social action is equally important; Matthew 25 says serving the poor is serving Christ; Christian Aid’s development work is mission without words). The 5-mark Explain question on Easter should cite 1 Corinthians 15:12–34 specifically — that is the named scripture anchor for why the resurrection matters to Christians. ‘Ecumenism’ and ‘evangelism’ are examinable technical terms — spelling them correctly earns SPaG marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The four spec pilgrimage sites are Jerusalem, Iona (Celtic spirituality), Taizé (ecumenical unity) and Walsingham (Marian, Catholic/Anglican); Luke 2:41–43 provides the biblical basis.
  • Easter is the central Christian festival celebrating the resurrection; 1 Corinthians 15:12–34 argues the resurrection is the foundation of all Christian hope.
  • Mission and evangelism (Mark 16:9–20) and care for the poor (Christian Aid; Matthew 25:31–46) are the two main expressions of the Church’s worldwide calling.

practice_questions.text: Outline three reasons why Christians go on pilgrimage.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete points, e.g. (1) To deepen faith by visiting the places where Jesus lived and died (Jerusalem); (2) For spiritual renewal and community (Iona, Taize); (3) As an act of penance, thanksgiving or seeking healing (Walsingham, Lourdes). Three separately identifiable reasons.

practice_questions.text: Describe what Christians celebrate during Holy Week.
practice_questions.marks: May include: Palm Sunday (entry into Jerusalem); Maundy Thursday (Last Supper, foot washing); Good Friday (crucifixion and death of Jesus); Holy Saturday (waiting); Easter Sunday (resurrection celebrated). Three accurate, relevant points.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways the local church serves its community.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed explanations. E.g. (1) Outreach work — local churches run food banks, debt counselling and community cafes, meeting practical needs in their area and putting Matthew 25 into practice; (2) Ecumenical partnership — local churches of different denominations work together on shared projects, expressing the prayer of Jesus for unity in John 17:21. Development required beyond naming the activity.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Easter is the most important Christian festival, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed points, at least one named source. E.g. (1) Easter celebrates the resurrection, which Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:17 calls the basis of all Christian faith — 'if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile'; (2) Easter marks the defeat of sin and death — it is the moment when Christ's atoning work on the cross is vindicated, giving Christians hope of their own resurrection. 5th mark requires a named source: 1 Corinthians 15:12–34.

practice_questions.text: Outline three differences between pilgrimage to Iona and pilgrimage to Jerusalem.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete points: (1) Jerusalem is the site of Jesus' death and resurrection — the most historically significant Christian site; Iona is a site of Celtic spirituality and social justice without direct gospel-history significance; (2) Jerusalem is shared by Christians, Jews and Muslims and has geopolitical complexity; Iona is a quieter, retreat-focused community site; (3) Jerusalem pilgrimage is ancient; Iona Community was founded in 1938 by George MacLeod.

practice_questions.text: 'The most important work of the worldwide Church is evangelism.' Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Both sides fully developed, named sources, explicit weighing, justified conclusion. FOR: the Great Commission (Mark 16:9–20) instructs disciples to 'go into all the world and proclaim the good news'; 1 Corinthians 15 shows the resurrection must be proclaimed; without evangelism the Church shrinks and cannot fulfil its purpose. AGAINST: Matthew 25:31–46 teaches that serving 'the least of these' is serving Christ — development work (Christian Aid) is equally central; actions speak louder than words; some argue that justice and reconciliation are the primary mission. Named sources: Mark 16:9–20; 1 Corinthians 15; Matthew 25:31–46. Secure (7–9). Developing (4–6). Emerging (1–3).

knowledge_checks.q: What is the Taize Community famous for?
options: It is England's national Marian shrine
It is an ecumenical community in France founded in 1940, drawing young Christians for prayer and unity
It is a Scottish island where St Columba founded a monastery in 563 CE
It is the site of Jesus' crucifixion and resurrection

knowledge_checks.q: What does 1 Corinthians 15:17 argue about the resurrection?
options: That the resurrection is a spiritual symbol of new life
That if Christ has not been raised, faith is 'futile'
That Christians will be raised at the Last Day in spiritual bodies only
That purgatory cleanses believers before the resurrection

knowledge_checks.q: Christian Aid is a development charity grounded in Matthew 25:31–46, which calls Christians to see Christ in 'the _____ of these.'
The four-week period of preparation before Christmas is called _____, beginning four Sundays before 25 December.
Match each pilgrimage site to its distinctive feature:
right: Site of Jesus' death and resurrection; holy to three religions
Scottish island; founded by St Columba in 563 CE; Celtic spirituality
Ecumenical French community founded 1940; young people; unity chants

flashcard_questions.q: Who founded the Iona Community and when?
flashcard_questions.a: George MacLeod, 1938 — on the island where St Columba founded a monastery in 563 CE.

flashcard_questions.q: Who founded the Taize Community and when?
flashcard_questions.a: Brother Roger Schutz, 1940 — an ecumenical community in France.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Taize known for in Christian worship?
flashcard_questions.a: Simple, repetitive chants that promote ecumenical unity; tens of thousands of young people visit annually.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 1 Corinthians 15:17 say about the resurrection?
flashcard_questions.a: If Christ has not been raised, 'your faith is futile and you are still in your sins.'

flashcard_questions.q: What is the liturgical season of Advent?
flashcard_questions.a: The four-week period of preparation and expectation before Christmas.
The final week before Easter, from Palm Sunday (entry into Jerusalem) to Easter Sunday (resurrection).

flashcard_questions.q: What does Matthew 25:31–46 teach about mission?
flashcard_questions.a: Serving 'the least of these' (the poor, sick, imprisoned) is serving Christ himself.
A Christian development charity operating in over 40 countries, tackling poverty grounded in Matthew 25.
The movement for visible unity between different Christian denominations.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Gospel passage grounds the Great Commission for Christian mission?
flashcard_questions.a: Mark 16:9–20 — 'Go into all the world and proclaim the good news.'

flashcard_questions.q: What makes Jerusalem significant for Christian pilgrims?
flashcard_questions.a: It is the site of Jesus' crucifixion, burial and resurrection — the central events of Christian salvation.

glossary_terms.definition: A journey to a sacred place undertaken for spiritual purposes, including deepening faith, penance, thanksgiving or seeking healing.
The four-week period of preparation and expectation before Christmas, beginning four Sundays before 25 December.
The final week of Lent, beginning on Palm Sunday (entry into Jerusalem) and ending on Easter Sunday, encompassing the events of Jesus' passion.
The Church's calling to spread the Gospel throughout the world, making disciples of all nations.
The specific act of proclaiming the Christian Gospel to those who have not yet heard or believed it, with the aim of making converts.
The movement for the visible unity of different Christian denominations, expressing the prayer of Jesus in John 17:21 that his followers 'may be one.'
A major international Christian development charity, founded in 1945, working in over 40 countries to tackle poverty and injustice.
